h1: Writing a brewery email newsletter that people actually open
title: Writing a Brewery Email Newsletter | Craft Beer School
desc: How to build and write a brewery email newsletter in India that people open: getting consent, what to send, subject lines, frequency and what to measure.
teaser: Instagram decides who sees your posts. An email list is the one audience a brewery actually owns.
standfirst: Social platforms change their rules every few months. A brewery's email list stays put. Here is how to build one with proper consent and write emails your drinkers look forward to.
sections: Why a brewery needs its own list

Most Indian breweries put their marketing effort into Instagram, with good reason. It is where drinkers discover beer. The platform decides how many followers see each post, though. Alcohol content is often shown to fewer people or restricted. An email list is different. When someone signs up, your message reaches their inbox every time, unless they choose to leave.

For a brewpub, that list is the people most likely to come back for a new release, an event or a festival. Even a few hundred engaged subscribers can fill a taproom on a quiet weeknight.

An email tool also gives you something social media rarely does: a clear record of who acted. You can see which beer announcements got clicks and which events filled. Over a year, that record is a better guide to your regulars than any follower count.

India's data protection law requires clear consent for collecting and using personal data. It gives people rights over how their data is used. Ask explicitly, explain what you will send and make leaving easy. Do not add people from your POS or booking system without their permission. Take advice on the details, because the rules are still being applied in practice.

Because this is alcohol, only invite adults above the legal drinking age, which varies by state. A simple age confirmation on the sign-up form is a sensible minimum.

Good places to collect sign-ups: a QR code on the menu and coasters, a sign-up card at the bar, the website, festival stalls and event bookings. Offer something useful in return, such as early news of releases or invitations to tasting nights, rather than discounts on alcohol, which may run into state promotion rules.

People open brewery emails for news they cannot get elsewhere. Good content includes:

  • New and returning beers, with a short note on taste and when they go on tap.
  • Events, such as quiz nights, brewer talks, food pairings and tap takeovers.
  • A look behind the scenes, such as a brew day, a new hop arriving or why a beer is late.
  • Something to learn, such as a style explained in a few lines or a food pairing idea.

Keep each email to one main story and two or three short items. Most people read on a phone. Our guide to seasonal and limited releases covers how to build a release calendar that gives your newsletter a natural rhythm.

The subject line decides whether the email is opened. Be specific: "Mango sour on tap Friday" beats "This week at the brewery". Avoid capital letters and too many exclamation marks, which look like spam and may be filtered.

Write in your brand voice, as one person writing to a regular. A short note from the head brewer feels more real than a corporate announcement. Our guide to brewery brand voice helps keep the tone consistent.

Send when you have something to say. Keep a steady rhythm. For most brewpubs, every two weeks or once a month works. Weekly works if you have weekly news. Sending nothing for three months then three emails in a week trains people to ignore you.

A real taproom detail: send event emails on Tuesday or Wednesday for a weekend event. Earlier and people forget. Later and plans are already made.

Watch a few numbers in your email tool:

  • Open rate shows whether subject lines and timing work. Treat it as a rough guide, because some email apps report opens unreliably.
  • Click rate shows whether the content gets people to act.
  • Unsubscribes tell you when an email missed the mark.

Then connect the email to something in the taproom. Ask guests how they heard about an event, or offer a small non-alcohol reward for mentioning the newsletter. That tells you more than any dashboard.

A brewery newsletter does not need fancy design. A clean template in brand colours, a good photo and short paragraphs are enough. Spend the time on content, not layout. Plain text emails from the head brewer often do as well as designed ones, because they read like a note from a person. The breweries with the best newsletters are usually the ones with the most interesting things happening and someone who enjoys writing about them.
faqs: How often should a brewery send a newsletter?
Every two weeks or monthly suits most brewpubs. Send weekly only if you have weekly news worth reading.
Can I add customers from my POS to the email list?
Not without their clear consent. India's data protection law requires permission to use personal data, so ask people to opt in.
What should a brewery email subject line say?
Something specific and useful, such as the beer or event and the day. Vague subject lines get ignored.
